174.history: A Tuathaich village on the old road the north calls Rathad nan Cairtearan, between Cnoc ghorm and the low ground short of Inis àrsaidh. When Comhairle na Slighe-iarainn would not carry the north's wool in the fortieth and forty-first years, the carts went south through it five days to Fèill Muileann òg, and a widow of the village who had fed carters at her own table for two winters, her husband lost under the western pits, began to take payment and keep a lamp lit past every other house's hour; it was the first inn on the road, and two more households lit lamps within the season. Daniel Frayne lodged under her lamp and learned from her the road's northern name, and her husband was the first name entered in Clàr nan Leòn. A carter from beyond it brought Walter Hale the last grievance he settled. Its druid house opened again in the forty-seventh year with Baile gharbh's.
174.known_for: the first lamp on Rathad nan Cairtearan

60.history: A harbour of the northern coast, deep enough for a hull of any size the north was likely to want and far enough from the southern yards that no guild master troubled to ride up and ask under what charter it worked. Its boats sailed with Mary Coyle to Seann Bhral in the twenty-fifth year, and its fishermen walked to Walter Hale's burial. In am Faoilleach of the forty-first year the Tuathaich shipwrights turned out of the southern guild yards came together here to lay a keel on the open strand, Harry Marlow cutting it to the humans' old lines, low and full in the bow; the hull went up on evenings and Sabbaths, and by an Cèitean of the forty-second year there was a shed over the slip and the place was called a yard. Its first hull took the water clean, swifter than anything the south had launched in a long season.

411.history: A shire of the drove road where the ground failed once before in the humans' time and was given a name for it that its people never forgot, Tiormachd Achadh shean, the drought of the old field. In the forty-third year the rains of am Màrt held off into an Cèitean and the wells of the drove road went brackish and then, three of them, dry to the stone. Its maor, a careful man who kept his own tally, wrote south before the second month of the dry was out, holding that a man argues with a poor harvest but a well gone to stone argues with no one, and cut twelve new wells along the road, one of them dry from the day it was dug on a dowser's word. The council answered faster than the north had ever known it to answer: grain from An Crùn's store at Cathair fhada reached the town's sidings by Slighe a' Ghuail on the morning the first proper rain fell.
411.known_for: the dry years and the grain by rail

131.history: The seat of a north-eastern shire whose old druid houses had stood roofless and silent since the humans first ruled there. Within half a year of Seonaid nic Ghill-Eathain's first lecture in the sacred wood, in the forty-seventh year, the houses of the shire at the town and at Àth fhada opened their doors on the old question again, and their teachers walked the better part of a week south to hear her before daring to teach it in their own halls, and did not miss a winter's walk after. The youngest of them, a woman not yet twenty on her first journey south, wrote of it in the school's own minute-book. Seonaid's sentence on the three stones was copied into every school's minute-book from Muileann chiar to this town.

197.history: A town near Coille Naomh Muileann chiar of Muileann chiar, where Scoiltean nan Draoidhean kept a wet-house for the months when the grove stood ankle-deep and no fire would stay lit under the bare oaks. Seonaid nic Ghill-Eathain took the house after her first winter's teaching, and in it her students argued the census line for fuil-ghuail by lamplight past the banking of the hearth. Three of them laid on its long table in the forty-ninth year slates copied from Colbh Cnoc chiar, Carragh Cnoc bheag and Calbh Cnoc ghorm, and found a mark like a bent reed and a straight double stroke on all three, which none could read. Catrìona nic Neacail came to teach here in the fifty-seventh year after resigning as surveyor-general, and the bell from Muileann dhearg's shut hall, bought on that shire's vote, rang in the school's tower to call her first lecture.
197.known_for: Scoiltean nan Draoidhean's wet-house, and the three slates

133.history: A harbour of the north-east coast, facing Caol gharbh across a strait that had drowned more boats in a hard winter than either town's harbour dues could bear. In the forty-eighth year the two shires joined their dues to pay for a breakwater across the strait between them, and laid its first stone that spring. It was eight years in the building and is the longest yet built on the island.

92.history: A harbour town of the south-west coast. On the twenty-third day of am Màrt in the fiftieth year a storm tide came into its lower town and drowned the net-lofts and the rope-walk. The town did not ask An Crùn for the rebuilding: its own carpenters raised both a second time on driven piles a fathom above the old floor, with timber floated down the Abhainn ghorm from the woods above Àth gharbh, and the work was finished before the autumn herring. The lofts stand so now, and the town's own telling of it is that the sea taught it once what it would not trouble to teach twice.

167.history: A shire of the east. On the twenty-first day of an Giblean in the fiftieth year it opened a school in every one of its six parishes, the first shire on the island to do so entire and out of its own dues rather than Tional nan Tuathach's purse or a guild's charity. The last and smallest opened with eleven children and a teacher hired from Baile chiar, who had never taught so few; within two years the benches held twenty and she stayed past her term. The council sent a clerk to ask how a shire so far from its notice had found the coin, and was shown plain accounts in a plain hand, the dues that would have gone to a road never built turned to six rooms and six teachers, and asked nothing further.

422.history: A town of the hill and moor country where Sireadh na Dàrna Fèithe began. In the fifty-first year the first of Alasdair mac Ùisdein's shafts went down on the rise above it in stone that gave every hopeful sign, and was judged barren within the fortnight; a dozen of the forty-one dry shafts were sunk on its hills. An old digger of the town, who had cut peat there as a boy, told Catrìona nic Neacail that the shepherds called the ground am Fearann Falamh. In the fifty-second year the town brought its claim for spoiled grazing to the circuit court, two shepherds swearing that the search cost them more lambs in two years than wolves had in ten, and the court found for the town; Taigh Mhic Ùisdein let its stone hall to meet the damages. A Holy Age survey in an Leabharlann had named the same hills searched and barren long before.
422.known_for: the first of the forty-one shafts

241.history: A town of red-earth fields in the east, where the barley fails on the thin soils every few years; in A' Bhliadhna Acrach of the twelfth, families walked from it to the pit towns for wages paid in coin. Sireadh na Dàrna Fèithe ended on the moor south of it in the fifty-first year, the forty-first shaft striking water at a depth no vein had ever answered. The shafts were left uncovered; sheep fell into them the first winter, and before the next summer was out a child of the town fell into one and was not found until the day after. The parish book holds her name and the day. The shire met in the same low room where it had argued its dues and voted to fence every shaft on its ground at its own cost, post and wire round every mouth, and entered a claim against Taigh Mhic Ùisdein for the fencing that was never paid.

202.history: A mill town south-east of the capital, where the grain of three shires had gone to be ground since before the humans came, its miller-families' mark cut into a millstone before any shire kept a chest for a charter. In the fifty-third year, with the vein-towns' grain orders thinned by scarce coin, the mills began for the first time in any keeper's memory to grind bark for the tanners of the coast instead of grain, and the families kept their mark and changed the trade under it without asking the Board's leave. The eldest miller, a woman near seventy, told a passing clerk that a wheel does not know what is under it, and that the grain would come back once the vein-towns had coin to buy it.
202.known_for: the mills that turned to bark

34.history: A town of the northern coast where Slighe a' Ghuail does not run, whose rope-walks take their hemp from the fields about Doire uaine and Achadh naomh by cart roads older than the survey lines. In the fifty-third year the restored custom chartered its rope-makers as a guild, the last trade the humans never touched to be given a charter of its own. Asked to send the charter south to be filed, the shire keeper answered that it would stay in the shire's own chest, as every paper of the shire had stayed since the chest was locked, and sent south a list of what the chest held and no more. When an Leabharlann called in the shire chests in the sixty-sixth year the old keeper, who had held the key since before Mòrag nic Coinnich was born, burned the chest rather than send it, met the clerks at the gate the next morning with the smoke still on his coat, and paid the council's fine without argument or apology. It is the one shire record of the calling-in an Leabharlann never read.

30.history: The great port south-east of the capital. In the ninth year its shire closed the old burial ground at Cnoc dhìreach to new graves, the vines having split so many stones that no clear plot could be found without turning up someone else's dead. In the fifty-fourth year it opened a covered market over its old strand for the fish that came up from Seann Bhral in the south and from the eastern grounds, the first roof the port had raised over that trade, so that the buyers of the capital could stand dry-shod while they haggled; the strand's old traders grumbled at first and less once a wet winter let them keep a fire by the scales.

273.history: A market town on the deep river in the northern hill country. As the coal-towns' trade fell away its market became the market for the wool and hides of the hills, and in the fifty-seventh and fifty-eighth years its market day drew more carts than Fèill Muileann òg, a thing no one living could remember any market doing. A wool-buyer from its hills told Daniel Frayne of it at Tional nan Tuathach's table, and Frayne entered it in the room's ledger under no heading that fit, since it was not Moot business and yet seemed to him to be.
273.known_for: the market that passed the fair

212.history: A town of the northern pits. In the fifty-ninth year, when Comann nan Gualadairean had bound no apprentices for two years, its maor opened a school for the sons and daughters of hewers the guild would not bind, to teach them to read, to reckon and to survey, reasoning that a hewer's child shut out of the pit might follow his father's trade from the surface with a chain in place of a pick. He wrote for primers to Daniel Frayne, who bound forty copies at his own bench and sent them north on the first cart. The benches passed thirty within the year, though several of the first pupils had already gone south to the ports to hire as chain-hands.

12.history: A town of the eastern hills by a ford where its river fishers still bless their nets, whose Seann Spioradan house keeps the oldest folk rite on the island. Copper was found in the hills behind it in the sixtieth year, and the Board opened a working within the season with men laid off from An Sloc Mòr's thinning galleries. The house gave the copper no blessing, its keeper telling the Board's factor that copper dug for a wage was copper dug like any other stone. By the second summer the town had built a street of new stone houses for the miners on the slope above the ford and named it, before the last house had a roof, for the pit they had come from, Sràid an t-Sluic; the miners kept small lumps of An Sloc Mòr's coal among their goods, and the house's keeper told the council a street named for another town's mountain risked forgetting the ground it stood on.
12.known_for: the copper, and Sràid an t-Sluic

170.history: A tanning town of the south-west coast. When the panthers crossed the hill country near Baile dhomhain by Imrich nam Pantar in the sixty-second year, its tanners heard of it before the herders had finished counting their losses and sent buyers up into the hills within the fortnight for the hides of the cats the herders' dogs and spears brought down, at a price the herders judged fair. They cured the skins through the summer, and the next year's Fèill Muileann òg saw saddles and belts of panther-hide sold under the town's mark for the first time in any chronicler's memory; the price of the mark doubled twice before the fair's ten days were out.

192.history: A town of the north whose chronicle has been kept by one family through four generations without a council's asking, begun by a great-grandmother on the back of an unused rent-roll. When Mòrag nic Coinnich called in the shire chests in the sixty-sixth year, the family's eldest daughter packed the town's rolls and chronicle into two carts herself and rode them south rather than trust a hired carter, and unpacked them at Mòrag's own table. Mòrag entered it as the best-kept shire record an Leabharlann received.
192.known_for: the family chronicle of four generations

37.history: A town of the north that sent its chest willingly to an Leabharlann in the sixty-seventh year and asked, as no shire before it had, for a copy of everything the chest held to be returned. Mòrag nic Coinnich's clerks made the copy, a full transcription bound in the same hand and set beside the original before either left the shire's hall, and the shire's copy became the pattern every later copy an Leabharlann made was cut to.

269.history: A pit town of the western hills, where Tuathaich hewers worked under the Board's overseers and scales. When the overseers left in the sixty-eighth year with the closing of the Àth leathan branch, the pits passed to the hewers, and they chose to keep the accounts Sam Varley, four-and-fifty, who had kept a private tally beside the Board's scale for eleven years. He opened a book of the pit's own accounts headed only with the day and the pit's name, the earliest page of the town's register of its pits, and his small son Tom carried the figures between the scale-house and his table. The carters who took Àth leathan's first coal to Seann Bhral by road passed through it.

9.history: A Tuathaich fishing harbour of the far north coast; boats were promised from its country to the second Fleadh na Mara at Cnoc ghorm. In the seventieth year, when the east-coast boats came north to the grounds the licence law kept for them and crowded the Tuathaich boats off the grounds nearest home, its boats took to the deep water beyond the northern isles, which no boat of that coast had fished in living memory for its roughness and the distance a crew had to keep from land. Two were lost the first year and none after, and before the next season was out its catch had passed Caol mhòr's.
9.known_for: the deep water beyond the northern isles

280.history: A town below the spoil-heaps of old coal galleries, never levelled, on the mountain where the council would not end the working of the vein by day and night. When coal-fuel doubled in price at the fair in the seventieth year, households of the town took to picking coal off the heaps to burn in their own grates, and in the seventy-first year the Board posted watchmen over the heaps. The watchmen were men of the town, and every night of the posting they saw nothing, though the heaps grew lower and the poorer grates burned warmer than the fair's price could have bought.
